title: How material advancements are leading the charge in the next generation of implantable bioelectronics
Harnessing Intermolecular Interactions to Boost Near-Infrared-II Fluorescence of Diketopyrrolopyrrole Nanoaggregates for In Vivo Imaging
authors: Zhisheng Gui; Jihao Li; Haitian Zhu; Xiuli Zheng; Liting Liu; Caihong Xiang; Fanda Meng; Lianrui Hu; Guangle Niu; Pengfei Wang
matched_keywords: nir-ii; photoacoustic imaging; in vivo imaging
abstract: Abstract Near-infrared (NIR)-II dyes hold tremendous potential for biomedical imaging and clinical applications. Structural modulation of fluorescent dyes has been widely recognized as a general approach to achieve NIR-II fluorescence. However, this strategy is often hindered by complex synthetic procedures and the obtained NIR-II dyes commonly suffer from aggregation-caused quenching. Herein, by rationally modulating intermolecular interactions, we facilely constructed two diketopyrrolopyrrole-based fluorescent dyes (DPP-2ANXF and DPP-2BTANXF) with NIR-II aggregate-state emissions. Compared with DPP-2ANXF, DPP-2BTANXF engineered with a stronger acceptor moiety showed intense red-shifted fluorescence of 970 nm with a quantum yield (QY) of 4.28% in low-polarity solution. Moreover, DPP-2BTANXF displayed strong NIR-II solid-state fluorescence with an emission peak at up to 1175 nm. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis and theoretical calculations revealed that the aggregated dimeric units are stabilized by multiple intermolecular interactions, leading to a narrowed energy gap. Through nanoprecipitation, DPP-2BTANXF was formulated into water-soluble nanoparticles (NPs) with NIR-I absorption and NIR-II emission (1108 nm) exhibiting a QY of 0.62%. DPP-2BTANXF NPs enabled high-contrast in vivo NIR-II fluorescence and photoacoustic imaging of mouse blood vessels, as well as imaging-guided surgical navigation of mouse tumor. Overall, this work provides an alternative strategy for developing versatile NIR-II fluorescent dyes for biomedical applications via rational modulation of intermolecular interactions.

title: Construction of a robust fluorescent probe for the rapid evaluation of natural products' inhibition of Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Xiao-Fang Xu; Xiu Xu; Li-Yi Zhou; Wan-Yi Wang; Min Ouyang; Jia-Xin Zheng; Lin Zhang
abstract: Peroxynitrite (ONOO-) is a key oxidative stress biomarker for Alzheimer's disease (AD), and elevated levels of ONOO- in the brain directly reflect the extent of oxidative stress-induced damage in AD. To enable in situ real-time monitoring of ONOO-, this study designed and synthesized a ratiometric near-infrared fluorescent probe (BF) based on a D-π-A framework. The probe BF emits near-infrared fluorescence; upon interaction with ONOO-, BF's intrinsic ICT is weakened, causing a blue shift in its emission and resulting in a red-to-green ratio change. When applied to PC12 cells and AD model mice, BF enables real-time ratiometric imaging monitoring of changes in ONOO- levels within the cells and the mouse brain. Furthermore, through molecular docking, neobavaisoflavone (with curcumin as a control) was screened as an intervention drug; BF successfully monitored the real-time dynamic downregulation of ONOO-, and the signal recovery in the neobavaisoflavone group was superior to that in the curcumin group and the model group. This study established a rapid evaluation platform centered on real-time imaging with near-infrared ratiometric probes, which not only enables in situ dynamic monitoring of AD-related ONOO- but also provides an intuitive and reliable visualization method for the rapid assessment of the efficacy of anti-AD candidate drugs.

Microenvironment-Responsive Polyaniline− Gelatin Conductive Hydrogel Promotes Infected Diabetic Wound Healing by Modulating Skin-Resident Cells Behavior
authors: Xiaxi Pan; Fufen Li; Garang Suoan; Qingsu Cheng; Xinying Li; Zhilang Xu; Jimin Guo; Changdao Mu; Defu Li; Liming Ge
abstract: Abstract Diabetic wound healing is severely impaired by persistent inflammation, bacterial infection, impaired angiogenesis, and especially disrupted bioelectrical signaling. Conductive hydrogels can help restore local bioelectrical signal transmission and provide an attractive strategy for intractable wound healing by modulating the behaviors of bioelectrically responsive skin-resident cells. Here, we developed a glucose/pH-responsive polyaniline− gelatin conductive hydrogel (HGP@D) based on double dynamic covalent crosslinking of the imine bond and boronic ester bond for promoting the Staphylococcus aureus-infected full-thickness diabetic wound healing. The HGP@D hydrogel had strong mechanical property, great tissue adhesive strength, glucose/pH dual-responsive drug release behavior, alongside robust broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, and potent intracellular antioxidation. The HGP@D hydrogel restored local bioelectrical signaling and created an anti-inflammatory wound microenvironment, thereby modulating the behaviors of skin-resident cells involved in diabetic wound repair, including fibroblast migration, macrophage M2-like polarization, and endothelial angiogenic activity. Mechanistic analyses suggested that the HGP@D hydrogel promoted infected diabetic wound healing through two Ca2+-associated regulatory axes: the Ca2+/CaMKKβ/AMPK/NF-κB axis for inflammatory regulation and the Ca2+/PI3K/Akt/mTOR/HIF-1α/VEGF axis for angiogenesis and tissue reconstruction. Overall, HGP@D provides a promising clinical therapeutic strategy for the advanced healing of diabetic wounds and other non-healing wounds by integrating glucose/pH-responsive microenvironment regulation with bioelectrical modulation.

title: Mechanistic insights into protein-mediated Zinquin fluorescence
authors: Natalie B. Schulte; Addison M. Duda; Sara M. Tuck; Kelly N. Chacón; Benjamin G. Bobay; Michael J. Therien; Andrew M. Dale; Katherine J. Franz
abstract: Zinquin (ZQ) is a small-molecule fluorescent probe used to monitor labile zinc in biological systems based on green fluorescence emission arising from the formation of [Zn(ZQ) 2 ] 2– complexes. However, studies in cells and protein-rich environments frequently report a pronounced blue-shifted emission, suggesting alternative interaction modes that complicate the interpretation of zinc imaging experiments. The nature of the interactions driving the blue shift is not fully understood. Here, we use the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 as a chemically and structurally well-defined model to elucidate the molecular origins of ZQ fluorescence in a zinc-binding protein. The NDM-1 has two distinct Zn 2+ ions in its active site, enabling direct assessment of zinc speciation, enzymatic activity, and structural integrity. Through an integrated approach combining fluorescence spectroscopy, enzyme activity assays, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and nuclear magnetic resonance, we identify two sources of ZQ fluorescence for this protein: formation of [Zn(ZQ) 2 ] 2– by stripping the weaker bound zinc, and a zinc-mediated ternary complex formed by NDM-1, Zn 2+ , and ZQ. This 1:1:1 complex localizes at the higher affinity zinc-binding site, where ZQ interacts concurrently with protein-bound zinc and specific residues of the NDM-1 active site. These nonpolar interactions generate a blue-shifted emission that is spectroscopically distinct from free zinc–ZQ complexes. This study characterizes the ternary complex that drives a protein-mediated fluorescence mechanism for ZQ and highlights the need to consider probe–protein interactions when interpreting fluorescent signals in chemical biology studies.
